title: Seoul's Climate Targets
inOneSentence: This slide shows Seoul's main climate plan: cut the city's emissions to half of the 2005 level by 2033, reach net zero by 2050, and push polluting cars out step by step.
background: Seoul's current climate plan is called the Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth in Seoul. It is a 10-year plan. It starts from the amount of greenhouse gas the city gave off in 2005, which was 52.34 million tons of CO₂e, and every emissions target is measured against that 2005 number.

The plan has two big targets. The first is to cut emissions to half of the 2005 level by 2033. The second is to reach carbon neutrality, also called net zero, by 2050. Net zero means that whatever gas the city still gives off is balanced by gas taken back out of the air, so the total comes to zero. The bars between 2005, 2033 and 2050 follow a straight path only to make the picture easy to read. The plan sets the 2033 and 2050 targets and does not promise a straight path between them.
There is no recent total for Seoul's emissions in English sources, so you cannot say how far along the city is today. Stay with the 2005 starting point and the two targets.

Buildings cause about two-thirds of Seoul's emissions, and buildings and transport together cause 85%. So after buildings, cars are the next big piece. Korea rates vehicles on an emission scale, and Grade 5 is the most polluting group. Grade 5 diesel vehicles are already banned citywide from December to March and all year in central Seoul. The plan then adds one step at a time: Grade 4 diesel vehicles out of central Seoul's green transport zones in 2025, Grade 4 vehicles banned citywide in 2030, gas and diesel cars banned from central Seoul in 2035, and banned citywide in 2050. The plan was written with 2025 as a future date, and your sources do not say how that step was carried out, so call it the planned 2025 step.

The plan also aims for 279,000 electric vehicles by 2033, the same year as the halfway emissions target. The car bans are a useful reminder that Seoul uses firm rules as well as rewards. Its reward approach is strongest on existing buildings, which is where the talk goes next.

explainSimply: Think of it like paying down a debt that starts from one known number. In 2005 Seoul put out 52.34 million tons of greenhouse gas. The plan says get down to half of that by 2033, and to net zero by 2050, where anything still given off is balanced out. The car bans are the steps along the way, with one more kind of polluting car pushed out every few years.
sayThis: By 2035, Seoul plans to ban gas and diesel cars from downtown.

questions.q: Is Seoul on track to cut its emissions in half by 2033?
questions.a: I couldn't find a recent total for Seoul's emissions in English sources, so I can't say. What I can show is the 2005 starting point of 52.34 million tons and the targets. For the whole country, Korea's emissions were 691.6 million tons in 2024, down about 2% from the year before, but that number covers all of Korea and doesn't tell us about Seoul.

questions.q: Why talk about cars in a talk about buildings?
questions.a: Buildings cause about two-thirds of Seoul's emissions, and buildings and transport together cause 85%. So transport is the next biggest piece after buildings. The car bans also show that Seoul uses firm rules as well as rewards.

questions.q: What do Grade 4 and Grade 5 mean?
questions.a: In the plan, Grade 5 diesel vehicles are already banned citywide from December to March and all year in central Seoul, and Grade 4 vehicles are the next group it goes after. The grades come from Korea's emission rating for vehicles, and Grade 5 is the most polluting group.

questions.q: It's 2026 now. Did the 2025 ban actually start?
questions.a: The plan set 2025 as the date for banning Grade 4 diesel vehicles from central Seoul's green transport zones. My sources list it as a plan date and don't confirm how it was carried out. So I present it as the planned 2025 step.

questions.q: Does the 2035 ban include hybrid cars?
questions.a: My sources only say internal combustion engine vehicles. They don't say how hybrids are treated, so I'd need to check the city's own rules.

Don't say the bars show Seoul's real yearly emissions. The straight path between 2005, 2033 and 2050 is only for the picture.
Don't say "half of today's emissions." The target is half of the 2005 level.
Don't say "zero emissions by 2050." Say net zero or carbon neutral, which allows some emissions as long as they are balanced out.
Don't say gas and diesel cars are banned citywide in 2035. The 2035 ban covers central Seoul. The citywide ban is planned for 2050.
Don't present the 2025 Grade 4 ban as confirmed and in force. Call it the planned 2025 step.
Don't mix up Seoul's city target with Korea's national target, which is a 40% cut from 2018 levels by 2030.
Don't use figures from seoulvision2030.com or 2030seoulplan.com. They look like unofficial sites. Use the city government or Seoul Solution.

title: One Less Nuclear Power Plant
inOneSentence: This slide explains Seoul's program to save or produce as much energy as one nuclear reactor makes in a year, and how it reached that goal six months early.
background: Two events in 2011 led to this program. The Fukushima nuclear disaster happened in Japan, and Seoul had a blackout the same year. In 2012 Seoul started a program called One Less Nuclear Power Plant. The idea was that the city could save or produce the same amount of energy that one power plant makes, so it would need one less plant.

The Phase 1 goal was 2 million TOE, which the city compared to the yearly output of one nuclear reactor. TOE means ton of oil equivalent. It is a unit that lets you add electricity, gas and other kinds of energy into one number. The plan split the goal into two parts: 1.59 million TOE from using less energy and 410,000 TOE from new renewable energy. Those are the 79% and 21% on the slide.

Seoul reached 2.04 million TOE in June 2014, six months early. The most effective single measure was Eco-Mileage, a voluntary rewards program for saving energy at home. It made each household's energy use something people could see and compare, and it gave small rewards for cutting it. By June 2014 it had 1.68 million participants, and together they saved 190,000 TOE. The 1.68 million comes back on the last slide. The 3D diagram labels this part "1.68 million households plus building retrofits." Say "participants" out loud, because that is what the sources count.

Phase 2 ran from 2014 to 2020 with bigger goals, including 20% of Seoul's electricity made inside the city. C40, a network of large cities working on climate, reports 4.65 million TOE of energy cut from 2012 to 2017. Electricity made in Seoul went from 2.9% in 2011 to about 5%. C40 says 5% and the city says 5.5% by 2015, so say it roughly doubled. That is still far below the 20% goal. The city set up the Seoul Energy Corporation to carry the work forward.

Korea still makes only 22.1% of its own energy (2024 figure), 35th of 38 OECD countries. Seoul made under 3% of its own electricity in 2011. That pressure helps explain why the city started by cutting how much energy it uses, and it asked residents to take part through programs like Eco-Mileage.

Seoul did the second thing at city scale. About four-fifths of the goal came from using less energy and about one-fifth from new renewable energy.

questions.q: Is 2 million TOE really what one nuclear reactor makes?
questions.a: That comparison comes from Seoul's own plan, and I use it the way the city did, to show the size of the goal. A power plant's output can be counted in more than one way, for example the fuel it burns or the electricity it sends out, so I wouldn't defend it as an exact match. The solid number is the goal itself, 2 million TOE.

questions.q: How did Eco-Mileage get people to save energy?
questions.a: It made home energy use visible. Members could see how much they used and compare it with before, and they earned small rewards for cutting it. By June 2014 it had 1.68 million participants who saved 190,000 TOE, and it was rated the most effective single measure in Phase 1.

questions.q: Did Phase 2 hit its targets?
questions.a: The goal was 20% of Seoul's electricity made in the city. The latest numbers I have are about 5% (the city says 5.5% by 2015), which is far from 20%. I didn't find a final 2020 figure. C40 also reports 4.65 million TOE of energy cut from 2012 to 2017, and that period includes Phase 1.

questions.q: Why did Seoul start with using less energy?
questions.a: Korea makes only 22.1% of its own energy (a 2024 figure), one of the lowest shares in the OECD, and Seoul made under 3% of its own electricity in 2011. After Fukushima and the 2011 blackout, the city chose to cut demand first. Most of the Phase 1 goal, 1.59 of the 2 million TOE, came from using less.

questions.q: Do the 79% and 21% describe the final result?
questions.a: They describe the planned split of the 2 million TOE goal. My sources give the total result, 2.04 million TOE, but no split for it. So I present the percentages as the plan.

title: Solar Panels on Balconies
inOneSentence: This slide covers Solar City Seoul, the 2017 program that put small solar panels on apartment balcony railings, with a goal of 1 GW more solar by 2022.
background: Solar City Seoul started in 2017. Its goals were 1 GW of new solar power by 2022 and solar for 1 million households. The budget was about ₩1.7 trillion, or about US$1.46 billion, and most of it was public money.

Seoul is a city of tall apartment blocks, so each apartment has very little roof. The city looked at balconies instead. It offered small standard solar kits that mount on the balcony railing. The kits were subsidized, renters could install them, and the city published design and safety standards for them. The target was 540,000 apartment balconies, plus 90,000 rental homes and 370,000 buildings. Those three parts add up to 1 million, the same as the household goal, though the dossier does not say that is how the goal was split.

By 2019 Seoul had 357.1 MW of solar across 285,000 households, and the program was described as ahead of its interim goal. 1 GW is 1,000 MW, so that is about a third of the way. A UN projection expected 583 MW by the end of 2020 and 1,015 MW by the end of 2022, but those were forecasts. Your sources do not give a final total for 2022.

The known barrier in Seoul was a lack of space on buildings and public facilities to put panels. Seoul also has a longer history of supporting small solar. In 2013 it became the first Korean city to pay small solar plants of 50 kW or less for each kWh they made, for five years.

For New York, the dossier calls balcony solar the idea New York could copy most directly. New York has hundreds of thousands of balconies, fire escapes and south-facing railings that make no power. The barriers are the building code, permits and landlord consent. New York would need a list of approved kits, a Department of Buildings process that doesn't require a full alteration filing for a plug-in kit, and a right for renters to install one. The dossier also points to Germany, where balcony solar spread quickly once permits got simpler.

questions.q: Why doesn't New York do this already?

questions.q: Who paid for it?
questions.a: Mostly the public. The program's budget was about ₩1.7 trillion, about US$1.46 billion, and the balcony kits were subsidized. My sources don't give the subsidy amount for each kit.

questions.q: Could New Yorkers put panels on fire escapes?
questions.a: Fire escapes are emergency exits, so anything on them would need to keep the way out clear, and that is a question for code officials. My sources list fire escapes among the surfaces that make no power today. I would start with real balconies and south-facing railings.

title: Paying for Building Retrofits
inOneSentence: This slide puts Seoul's low-interest retrofit loans next to New York's Local Law 97 limits and fines, which is the main comparison of the whole talk.
background: Buildings use 56% of Seoul's energy and cause about two-thirds of its emissions. Most of those buildings are already standing, so the big question is how to pay for fixing them. A retrofit means upgrading an existing building, for example with insulation, better windows, new lighting or a new heating and cooling system.

Seoul's answer is the Building Retrofit Project, or BRP, which started in 2008. In 2012 it grew under One Less Nuclear Power Plant and opened to private universities and hospitals, then to homes. The city lends owners money at a low interest rate to pay for upgrades. In 2013 the city cut the rate from 2.5% to 1.75% a year and raised the most it would lend from 80% to 100% of the eligible cost, so an owner did not have to pay the eligible cost up front. The stated target is 90,000 buildings, which is 20% of Seoul's buildings that are over 20 years old.

Results depend on the source, so always name it. C40 reports 25,841 tons of CO₂ saved from 2012 to 2015 across about 4,200 projects, and other C40 reporting says 72,000 buildings were improved. A city report says 20,000 buildings and houses and 192,234 TOE of energy saved. A measured sample of 100 buildings (2012 to 2013) found that homes used 10% less energy and other buildings 6.5% less. Separately, 59 welfare facilities (social service buildings) were retrofitted and saved about 15% of their average energy use.

New York's answer is Local Law 97, passed in 2019. It covers buildings over 25,000 sq ft. Each building gets a yearly carbon limit per square foot, set by its type of use, such as offices or apartment buildings. The law does not tell owners what to fix. If a building goes over its limit, the owner pays $268 for each ton of CO₂e over the limit, every year. The overall goal is a 40% cut by 2030 and 80% by 2050, from 2005 levels.

The limits get much tighter in 2030. The office limit drops by 64.5% and the apartment building limit by 50.4% compared with 2024 to 2029. About 11% of covered buildings are estimated to be over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% are projected to be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes. LL97 leaves it to owners to find the money for upgrades. That gap is the reason for your second recommendation, a New York city loan for LL97 upgrades on terms like Seoul's.

explainSimply: Imagine your building needs a new boiler and new windows. In Seoul, the city's retrofit loan was cut to 1.75% a year in 2013 and could cover the whole eligible cost, so the owner could start the work and pay it back over time. In New York, the city sets a carbon limit and sends a bill if the building goes over it. For example, a building 100 tons over its limit would pay 100 × $268, which is $26,800, every year until it gets under the limit.
sayThis: So my second idea for New York is a city loan for these upgrades, like Seoul's.

questions.q: If the loans are optional, why would owners in Seoul take one?
questions.a: The loan made the upgrade easier to start. In 2013 the city raised the loan to 100% of the eligible cost and cut the rate to 1.75% a year. The upgrades also cut energy use. In a measured sample of 100 buildings, homes used 10% less energy and other buildings 6.5% less, which means lower energy bills.

questions.q: How many buildings did the BRP actually reach?
questions.a: It depends on the source and what it counts. C40 reports about 4,200 projects from 2012 to 2015, other C40 reporting says 72,000 buildings, and a city report says 20,000 buildings and houses. So I give the range and name the source. The target was 90,000 buildings.

questions.q: Wouldn't fines work faster than loans?
questions.a: Fines set a clear deadline, and New York's target is the harder one. The problem is that a fine doesn't help an owner pay for the work, and about 63% of covered buildings are projected to be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes. That's why I suggest adding a Seoul-style loan to LL97, tied to meeting the limits.

questions.q: Does New York offer owners any financing?
questions.a: LL97 itself sets the limits and the fines and leaves the money to owners. In my research I didn't find a city loan like Seoul's BRP, though there may be smaller programs I didn't cover.

questions.q: Why does the share of buildings over the limit jump from about 11% to about 63%?
questions.a: Because the limits get much tighter in 2030. Compared with the 2024 to 2029 limits, the office limit drops by 64.5% and the apartment building limit by 50.4%. A building that passes today can be well over in 2030 without any change on its side.

dontSay: Don't give a single total for what the BRP achieved. Figures run from about 4,200 projects to 72,000 buildings depending on the source and the cutoff date.
Don't say the BRP reached its 90,000 building target.
Don't say 1.75% was the rate from the start. It was 2.5% until 2013.

Don't claim 1.75% is Seoul's rate today. It is the BRP rate set in 2013. Seoul's newer climate plan mentions long-term interest-free loans for upgrades, but the dossier has no details, so only mention that if asked.
Don't mix up 56% and two-thirds. 56% is buildings' share of Seoul's energy use, and about two-thirds (67%) is their share of emissions.
Don't say New York gives owners no help at all. Say LL97 leaves the financing to owners and you found no city loan like Seoul's.
Don't say LL97 tells owners which upgrades to make. It sets a carbon limit per square foot by building type and lets owners choose how to meet it.
Don't say 63% of buildings are over the limit now. About 11% are over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% are projected to be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes.
Don't mention LL97 carbon-credit trading starting in 2026. Only one weak source claims it.
Don't give numbers about the Empire State Building's own energy upgrades in the next photo. That is not in your dossier.

terms.meaning: Upgrading an existing building so it uses less energy, for example with insulation, new windows, lighting, or heating and cooling equipment.
Seoul's program, started in 2008, that lends building owners money at low interest to pay for retrofits.
The part of a project's cost that the loan program agrees to pay for.
New York's 2019 law, part of the Climate Mobilization Act, that sets yearly carbon limits for buildings over 25,000 sq ft and fines owners who go over.
The most greenhouse gas a building may give off per square foot each year under LL97. It depends on the building's type of use, called its occupancy group, such as office or multifamily.
A building with several separate homes, such as an apartment building.
Social service buildings, such as community or care centers.
Seoul Metropolitan Government, the city government of Seoul.

nycLink: This is the center of the talk and the source of your main recommendation, idea 02 on slide 19. New York already has the limits and the fines. What it lacks is a way to help owners pay for the work, and about 63% of covered buildings could be over the 2030 limits. The dossier's suggestion is a city loan fund on BRP terms (up to 100% of cost at 1.75%), tied to meeting LL97 limits, so an owner facing a fine has a way to pay for the fix. Seoul is weaker on the other side, since its loans are voluntary, so the comparison suggests each city could use what the other has.

title: Two Older Buildings
seoul: An older building in downtown Seoul (the photo picked so far is Sewoon Sangga, a long concrete building near Euljiro; check the caption on the slide). It is shown as older building stock. Your sources don't say it had a BRP energy retrofit, so don't call it a BRP building. The BRP target is 90,000 buildings, 20% of Seoul's buildings over 20 years old.
nyc: The Empire State Building in Midtown Manhattan. It is far over 25,000 sq ft, so Local Law 97 covers it, and the owner pays for any upgrades it needs to stay under its limit.
why: Both are large older buildings of the kind that need upgrades. In Seoul the city lends money for that work, and in New York the owner pays and faces fines for going over the limit.
